title: Regional price adjustments offer a more nuanced view of consumer strength
gist: Oxford Economics argues that nominal income and spending data systematically misrank consumer markets, and is building an internal city-level price-level model (adapted from a 2019 OECD methodology, fitted on US metro data) to extend PPP adjustment below the national level. Applied, it shows St. Louis purchasing power ($75,700) marginally ahead of Washington, DC ($73,600) despite far lower nominal pay, and Warsaw and Prague PPP-adjusted incomes now level with Brussels, Lyon, and Bristol.

insights.claim: Purchasing power of a local market is a better gauge of living standards and consumer strength than nominal incomes or nominal spending, which is the core reason cross-city consumer comparisons based on headline pay are unreliable.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Consumer-exposed revenue models ranked on nominal per-capita income are mis-sorting target markets; re-rank on price-adjusted income before sizing store, hiring, or ad-spend footprints.
insights.quote: The purchasing power of a local market tells a more meaningful story than nominal incomes or spending alone—and it’s also a better gauge of living standards.

themes.theme: US metro test case: DC vs St. Louis inversion

insights.claim: Washington, DC is one of the most expensive US metros, with average prices 12% above the US average, which cuts the real value of local incomes substantially.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: A 12% price premium is a direct haircut on real wage growth and consumer discretionary spend in one of the highest nominal-income US metros.
insights.quote: Washington, DC, is one of the most expensive metros in the country, with average prices 12% higher than the US average.
insights.locator: As one of the few countries that publishes regional price-level data

insights.claim: Adjusting for local price levels inverts the US metro income ranking between Washington, DC and St. Louis: DC's $82,500 average 2025 income falls to $73,600 in US-average price terms, while St. Louis's lower $72,000 income rises to $75,700 — putting St. Louis marginally ahead.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Screening US metros on nominal income for consumer expansion or site selection can rank a market backwards; lower-cost Midwest metros carry more real spending capacity than headline pay implies.
insights.quote: Adjusted for purchasing power, an income of $72,000 here is equivalent to $75,700, which is actually marginally ahead of Washington, DC.

insights.claim: Despite very different average pay packets, how far income stretches in Washington, DC and St. Louis is almost identical, making lower-nominal-income metros more attractive as places to live and work than they first appear.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Supports the case for labour-market and consumer-demand migration toward lower-cost metros — relevant to regional housing, retail footprint, and remote-work relocation theses.
insights.quote: St. Louis in this example emerges as a more attractive place to live and work than it might first seem.

insights.claim: The US is one of the very few countries that publishes official regional price-level data, which is why it can serve as the calibration case for sub-national purchasing-power analysis.

insights.so_what: The data monopoly means any non-US city-level purchasing-power series is modelled, not measured — check the estimation method before trusting European city rankings.

themes.theme: Building a modelled city-level price series

insights.claim: The main structural weakness of standard PPP adjustment is that it is computed at national level while consumer markets are better understood at city level, and cost-of-living differences within a country can be as pronounced as those between countries.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: National PPP series used as a proxy for city-level demand introduce error large enough to flip market rankings — a modelling gap worth pricing into country-level consumer forecasts.
insights.quote: PPP is typically calculated at the national level, when consumer markets are often better understood at the city-level.
insights.locator: Developing a measure of regional price differences

insights.claim: Oxford Economics is developing internal estimates of relative price levels between cities by adapting a methodology first explored by OECD researchers in 2019, fitting the relationship between economic drivers and average price levels across US metropolitan areas and then predicting relative price levels in other geographies including European cities.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: A new commercial dataset in development — watch for its release as an input for city-level consumer market sizing where official data does not exist.
insights.quote: we have been developing our own internal estimates of relative price-level differences between cities, adapting a methodology first explored by OECD researchers in 2019

insights.claim: The two explanatory drivers named in the city price-level model are income per person and housing costs as a share of total spending, meaning housing burden is treated as a primary determinant of a city's general price level.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Housing-cost share becomes a tradeable proxy for a city's real consumer squeeze; cities with rising housing share should see modelled price levels rise and real spending power fall.

themes.theme: CEE convergence: Warsaw and Prague reach Western parity

insights.claim: Central and Eastern European cities such as Warsaw and Prague have been, and are expected to remain, hotspots for consumer spending growth across Europe, driven by booming local economies and rising incomes.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Directs consumer-facing capital allocation toward CEE metros as the structural growth pocket in an otherwise low-growth European consumer market.
insights.quote: Central and Eastern European cities such as Warsaw and Prague have been, and are expected to remain, hotspots for consumer spending growth across Europe
insights.locator: Our analysis also tells an interesting story about European convergence

insights.claim: Although nominal incomes in Warsaw and Prague remain much lower than in Western Europe, their PPP-adjusted average incomes are now on a par with Brussels, Lyon, and Bristol — a result described as almost unthinkable 20 years ago.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: CEE consumer addressable market is far larger in real terms than nominal-income screens show; a re-rating input for retail, QSR, and consumer brands expanding east.
insights.quote: the average PPP-adjusted incomes in these cities are now on a par with peers like Brussels, Lyon, and Bristol. This would have been almost unthinkable 20 years ago

insights.claim: Income and spending-power parity is explicitly not the same as full living-standards convergence, since many other components contribute to quality of life beyond incomes and spending power in Warsaw and Prague relative to Western cities.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Caps the convergence trade: PPP parity supports consumer-demand theses but not talent-attraction or premium-services theses in CEE.
